subtype: Testing the excuse [Response]
passage:
I'm Mohit, and I share a flat in Andheri with Divyansh. For a week he had been explaining why he wasn't applying for the Singapore posting his firm had offered: the humidity, his mother's knees, the role "wasn't really strategic", a better opening might come next year. Each version was longer than the last.
On Sunday night I found him at the dining table with an index card. He wrote one line, covered it with his hand, then looked up. "Mohit, if I heard all those reasons from you, would I believe them?"
"Honestly? No."
He turned the card over. It said: I'm scared I'll be out of my depth there.
Nine words. He stared at it a long time. I don't know everything he felt, but his shoulders dropped, as if something heavy had been set down. On Monday he booked a call with the manager who'd offered the role, to ask what support new people got.

qa.q: What did Divyansh write on the index card?
qa.a: I'm scared I'll be out of my depth there.

qa.q: Why might the long list of reasons have felt more comfortable to Divyansh than the one line?
qa.a: The humidity, his mother's knees and next year made staying back sound sensible and even caring; the single line admitted fear, which is less flattering, so facing it took effort but brought relief.

qa.q: What turning point came from testing the excuse?
qa.a: Once the real reason was named as fear, Divyansh could act on it, booking a call to ask what support new people got instead of hiding behind the weather and next year.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Mohit to be asked, "would I believe them?"
qa.a: Mohit had to choose between being polite and being honest; answering "No" risked stinging a friend, but it gave Divyansh the push to turn the card over.

grounding: Shows, through a flatmate's eyes, an adult who writes the real reason for a choice and checks it against what they would accept from a friend, finding it short and unflattering.

Sunday. Swati texted her cousin Yogesh that she couldn't make his housewarming in Nashik. "Train timings are awful, I've got a deadline, and I think a cold is coming." She added a sad face and felt oddly pleased with how reasonable it sounded.
Tuesday. Clearing her desk, Swati found the message still open. She tried a trick her flatmate used: if Yogesh sent me these three reasons, would I buy them? No. She'd call it an excuse. So she opened the notes on her phone and typed the actual reason. Neha will be there, and I still owe her an apology. One line. Not flattering at all.
Friday. She called Yogesh. "The cold was an excuse. It's Neha. I've been avoiding her since last year."
Yogesh was quiet, then laughed softly. "Come anyway. I'll put you two on chai duty."
She booked the early train that night.

qa.a: Train timings were awful, she had a deadline, and she thought a cold was coming.

qa.q: Why did the three reasons feel convincing to Swati at first?
qa.a: Each was partly true and made her sound busy and sensible, which kept her away from the less flattering truth that she was avoiding Neha.

qa.a: Asking whether she would accept the same three reasons from Yogesh; when she knew she wouldn't, she typed the short, real reason and could act on it 🙂

qa.q: How might Yogesh have felt hearing the real reason on the phone?
qa.a: Yogesh might feel trusted and closer to Swati, and glad to know the true problem so he could help, instead of feeling brushed off with train timings.

grounding: Illustrates an adult who writes down the real reason for skipping a family event, tests her excuse against what she'd accept from someone else, and finds the honest reason shorter and less flattering.

Okay, Mahima, you asked, so. It was a pulmonary embolism. A clot, from his leg, that went up into his lung. Why are you looking at me like that? I'm fine. I'm just saying what happened. Mum keeps crying in the kitchen and I keep reading. It makes more sense to me this way.

"So, Mitali, I've worked it out. Asif has an avoidant attachment style, I lean anxious. When I asked for more time together, he withdrew, I pushed, and the cycle fed itself. It's textbook." Her notebook lay open on her knees: a diagram, arrows in two colours.

Dear Ritu,
You asked how I'm coping since Shanta teacher died. Honestly, at first I did what I do in every lab: I made a timeline. When she first mentioned feeling tired, when she stopped coming to Sunday class, when her daughter called us. Writing it down helped. I understood it wasn't sudden, and that she had chosen to keep teaching as long as she could.
But I noticed I kept adding details and never once felt anything. So on Sunday I blocked an hour, five to six, like a class. I sat on the floor with her old harmonium book, the one with her pencil notes in the margins, and read them. By the third page I was crying properly, for the first time.
The timeline wasn't wasted. It told me what I was sad about. I think I needed both.
Write back soon,
Kalyani

You want to know how I've been since Bauji passed, Nirmala? Okay.
First week, I was all spreadsheet. Every doctor's visit, every report, the dates his medicines changed. I understood the illness better than anyone in the family. Chacha kept ringing me, "Gurpreet beta, what did the doctor mean?", like I was the expert. It felt good to be useful.
Then one night I caught myself reading about kidney function at two in the morning, and realised I hadn't once said I missed him. Not to anyone. Not even to myself.
So I made a rule. Every evening, after the reading, fifteen minutes with his old radio, tuned to the station he liked. No phone, no notes. First evening, nothing. Second, nothing. Third evening the old film songs came on and I just broke.
I think the reading was me walking toward it slowly. The radio was where I finally got there.

Mentor's notes, Sunaina, Thursday
Aniket, from my old team, was laid off in the restructuring two weeks ago. We still meet every Thursday.
Today he walked me through it like a case study: "Revenue dipped eight percent, they cut the newest hires in two units, it's statistically sensible." Clear, calm, well argued.
What I noticed: he hasn't eaten at our last three meetings; he orders black coffee and leaves the sandwich. He mentioned he'd "optimised" his sleep to five hours so he could apply for more roles. His laptop stayed open the whole time, thirty-one tabs.
What I did: I closed my own notebook and asked, "Not what it means. How does it feel?" He began explaining the market again, stopped, and said, "Like I got thrown out." We sat with that. I bought him a proper lunch and he ate half.
Next: meet again Monday, not Thursday.

Sat, 11 pm
Met Gopika for chai at the old press club canteen, first time since the paper shut the features desk. She was so composed. She talked about ad revenue, falling print numbers, how "any rational editor" would have cut features first. She even drew me a little graph on a napkin.
But her eyes had dark rings, she admitted she'd been up till four most nights "reading industry reports", and she said she'd mostly been living on tea. Her samosa went cold on the plate.
I almost argued with the graph. Instead I said, "That all makes sense. But how does it feel, Gopika?" She folded the napkin into smaller and smaller squares. Then: "Like all those years of wanting this job just... vanished." Her voice cracked. We stayed till the canteen closed.
I'll call her Tuesday. Just to check in.
Sangeeta

In their rented room in Salt Lake, Payal was ironing a kurta for Saturday's open-mic poetry night. "Come with me, Indu. Just to listen."
Indu didn't look up from her accounting textbook. "Please. Standing up and reading your diary to strangers? It's so self-obsessed. Everyone snapping their fingers like it's deep." Her voice sharpened. "Honestly, it's embarrassing, Payal. Grown people fishing for claps."
Payal set the iron down. "That was a lot. I only asked if you wanted to come."
"I'm just being honest."
After Payal left, Indu sat very still. Then she slid a thin blue notebook out from under her mattress. Its pages were full of short lines about her grandmother's kitchen, the metro at night, the ache of leaving home. She read one under her breath, the way people did on stage, and quickly shut it.

qa.a: Under her mattress.

qa.q: Why might sneering at the open mic feel reasonable to Indu?
qa.a: Calling it self-obsessed keeps her own wish to share her poems safely hidden; if reading on stage is embarrassing, she never has to risk it.

qa.q: What choice is open to Indu after she reads a poem under her breath?
qa.a: She could admit to herself, and maybe to Payal, that part of her wants to go, and try simply listening at one open mic.

qa.q: What might Payal take away from saying "That was a lot"?
qa.a: Payal noticed the reply was far harsher than a simple invitation deserved, and may feel stung and puzzled about why Indu cares so much.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult who scorns open-mic poetry with unusual heat while secretly writing poems, the intensity pointing to the opposite pull.

subtype: Over-the-top praise from a rival [Observer]

At the cooperative bank branch in Kuttanad, the news came on Monday: Kiran would be the new branch manager. Francis, who had also applied, was the first to shake Kiran's hand.
By Wednesday Samir had lost count. Francis praised Kiran at the tea stall, at the counter, in front of farmers waiting with loan forms. "Best decision head office ever made. Kiran is a born leader, honestly." On Thursday he said it twice in one conversation, and his laugh came a beat too fast.
The clerk, Molly, muttered to Samir, "All that sugar. He must be plotting something."
Samir wasn't so sure. Francis had wanted that post for three years. Maybe the praise was a way of swallowing disappointment in public. Maybe some of it was real.
"Let him be," Samir said. After closing, Samir walked out with Francis to the boat jetty and just asked how the week had been.

qa.a: Kiran would be the new branch manager.

qa.q: What might Francis be feeling beneath the constant praise?
qa.a: Francis may be swallowing real disappointment after wanting the post for three years; the extra praise could be a way to look gracious while hurting, though some of it may be sincere.

qa.q: Which choice by Samir seems wiser than Molly's guess?
qa.a: Samir didn't treat the gushing as proof of plotting; Samir let it be and simply asked Francis how the week had been, leaving room for honest mixed feelings.

qa.q: How might Kiran experience all this praise?
qa.a: Kiran might feel flattered but a little uneasy, sensing that so much praise from a rival for the same post is hard to read.

grounding: Shows a colleague who notices a rival praising a promotion too much and too often and reads it as a hint of mixed feelings, not proof of ill will.

subtype: Over-the-top praise from a rival [Observer]
passage:
At the vet clinic in Auckland, the staff-room whiteboard now read CONGRATS LUKAS, HEAD NURSE! in Nadia's handwriting, with three hearts.
Nadia had applied for the same job. Since Monday she had baked Lukas a lemon cake, told two clients he was "the best thing that ever happened to this place", and repeated at every handover, "Honestly, they chose perfectly."
Stacking towels, Xin's first thought was that it sounded almost like sarcasm. Then Xin remembered Nadia crying quietly in the car park after her interview, and thought again. Too much, too often, yes. But that could be someone trying hard to be glad while also being sad.
On Thursday Xin found her in the dispensary, straightening boxes that were already straight, and handed her a coffee. "It's allowed to sting a bit, you know."
Nadia let out a long breath. "Is it that obvious?"

qa.a: CONGRATS LUKAS, HEAD NURSE!, in Nadia's handwriting, with three hearts.

qa.q: Why did Xin stop thinking the praise sounded like sarcasm?
qa.a: Remembering Nadia crying in the car park after the interview made Xin think the extra praise came from trying to be glad while still feeling sad, not from spite.

qa.q: Which choice by Xin in the dispensary helped most?
qa.a: Offering a coffee and gently saying it was allowed to sting, without accusing, gave Nadia room to admit the mixed feelings 🙂

qa.q: How might Lukas feel about all the praise from Nadia?
qa.a: Lukas may enjoy the warmth but also feel a bit awkward, knowing Nadia wanted the same job and not being sure what the praise really means.
